reference: B. Zitkovich, T. Yu, S. Xu, P. Xu, T. Xiao, F. Xia, J. Wu, P. Wohlhart, S. Welker, A. Wahid et al., “RT-2: Vision-language-action models transfer web knowledge to robotic control,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2023, arXiv:2307.15818.
summary: RT-2 represents robot actions as tokens and co-trains on robotic trajectories and vision-language tasks. It studies how knowledge learned from web data transfers into language-conditioned manipulation.

reference: M. J. Kim, K. Pertsch, S. Karamcheti, T. Xiao, A. Balakrishna, S. Nair, R. Rafailov, E. Foster, G. Lam, P. Sanketi et al., “OpenVLA: An open-source vision-language-action model,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2024, arXiv:2406.09246.
summary: OpenVLA combines pretrained visual-language representations with autoregressive robot-action prediction in an open model. It provides a generalist manipulation policy that can be adapted to new tasks through fine-tuning.

reference: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, “Open X-Embodiment: Robotic learning datasets and RT-X models,” in Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. Robot. Autom. (ICRA), 2024, arXiv:2310.08864.
summary: Open X-Embodiment brings together robot demonstration datasets collected across different embodiments. The accompanying RT-X models examine whether training on this combined data improves transfer between robotic platforms.

reference: K. Black, N. Brown, D. Driess, A. Esmail, M. Equi, C. Finn, N. Fusai, L. Groom, K. Hausman, B. Ichter et al., “π0: A vision-language-action flow model for general robot control,” in Proc. Robot.: Sci. Syst. (RSS), 2025, arXiv:2410.24164.
summary: The π0 model couples a pretrained vision-language backbone to a flow-matching action expert. It generates continuous action chunks for manipulation across tasks and robot embodiments.

reference: J. Bjorck, F. Castañeda, N. Cherniadev, X. Da, R. Ding, L. Fan, Y. Fang, D. Fox, F. Hu, S. Huang et al., “GR00T N1: An open foundation model for generalist humanoid robots,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.14734, 2025.
summary: GR00T N1 combines vision-language interpretation with diffusion-based action generation for humanoid robots. Its dual-system design connects slower semantic processing with continuous control.

reference: Gemini Robotics Team, “Gemini Robotics: Bringing AI into the physical world,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.20020, 2025, google DeepMind technical report.
summary: Gemini Robotics extends a Gemini vision-language model to generate robot actions from observations and instructions. The developer-reported study examines manipulation capabilities and transfer across embodiments.

reference: –––, “Gemini Robotics 1.5: Pushing the frontier of generalist robots with advanced embodied reasoning, thinking, and motion transfer,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.03342, 2025, google DeepMind technical report.
summary: Gemini Robotics 1.5 integrates embodied reasoning with action generation in a multi-embodiment policy. The developer report also describes transferring motion knowledge across robot configurations.

reference: M. J. Kim, C. Finn, and P. Liang, “Fine-tuning vision-language-action models: Optimizing speed and success,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.19645, 2025.
summary: OpenVLA-OFT studies fine-tuning choices for faster and more successful VLA control. Its recipe uses action chunking and parallel continuous regression instead of sequential action-token decoding.

reference: S. Fei, S. Wang, J. Shi, Z. Dai, J. Cai, P. Qian, L. Ji, X. He, S. Zhang, Z. Fei et al., “LIBERO-Plus: In-depth robustness analysis of vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.13626, 2025.
summary: LIBERO-Plus probes manipulation policies with controlled visual, physical-configuration, and instruction perturbations. Its instruction-removal and goal-replacement tests distinguish apparent language robustness from reliable instruction grounding.

reference: A. Jain, M. Zhang, K. Arora, W. Chen, M. Torne, M. Z. Irshad, S. Zakharov, Y. Wang, S. Levine, C. Finn et al., “PolaRiS: Scalable real-to-sim evaluations for generalist robot policies,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2512.16881, 2025.
summary: PolaRiS reconstructs interactive simulation environments from short scans of real scenes for robot-policy evaluation. Paired simulated and physical tests examine how well these evaluations predict real-world performance.

reference: H. Li, Y. Zuo, J. Yu, Y. Zhang, Z. Yang, K. Zhang, X. Zhu, Y. Zhang, T. Chen, G. Cui et al., “SimpleVLA-RL: Scaling VLA training via reinforcement learning,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Representations (ICLR), 2026, arXiv:2509.09674.
summary: SimpleVLA-RL adapts VLA policies through online reinforcement learning with stochastic action-token decoding. It evaluates how interaction changes performance under different demonstration budgets.

reference: S. Tan, K. Dou, Y. Zhao, and P. Krähenbühl, “Interactive post-training for vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.17016, 2025.
summary: RIPT-VLA fine-tunes pretrained robot policies through reinforcement learning with sparse task-success rewards. It studies interactive post-training of both lightweight and larger policies under limited supervision.

reference: M. Assran, A. Bardes, D. Fan, Q. Garrido, R. Howes, M. Komeili, M. Muckley, A. Rizvi, C. Roberts, K. Sinha et al., “V-JEPA 2: Self-supervised video models enable understanding, prediction and planning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.09985, 2025.
summary: V-JEPA 2 learns predictive video representations from action-free video at scale. Its separately adapted V-JEPA 2-AC model predicts action-conditioned latent transitions for planning toward image goals.

reference: J. Jang, S. Ye, Z. Lin, J. Xiang, J. Bjorck, Y. Fang, F. Hu, S. Huang, K. Kundalia, Y.-C. Lin et al., “DreamGen: Unlocking generalization in robot learning through video world models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.12705, 2025.
summary: DreamGen generates task-conditioned robot videos and obtains pseudo-action labels through inverse dynamics. The resulting synthetic trajectories augment policy training as an offline data-generation pipeline.

reference: D. Hafner, W. Yan, and T. Lillicrap, “Training agents inside of scalable world models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.24527, 2025.
summary: Dreamer 4 trains agents inside a scalable video world model learned from offline data. Its main application is Minecraft, while separate ablations examine the amount of action-labeled video required for prediction.

reference: J. Cen, C. Yu, H. Yuan, Y. Jiang, S. Huang, J. Guo, X. Li, Y. Song, H. Luo, F. Wang et al., “WorldVLA: Towards autoregressive action world model,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.21539, 2025.
summary: WorldVLA uses shared autoregressive modeling for robot actions and future observations. Its predictive-training experiments provide evidence about joint learning without establishing a general advantage for online candidate-action search.

reference: M. J. Kim, Y. Gao, T.-Y. Lin, Y.-C. Lin, Y. Ge, G. Lam, P. Liang, S. Song, M.-Y. Liu, C. Finn, and J. Gu, “Cosmos Policy: Fine-tuning video models for visuomotor control and planning,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Representations (ICLR), 2026, arXiv:2601.16163.
summary: Cosmos Policy adapts a video model to jointly generate actions, future states, and values. It evaluates direct visuomotor execution alongside rollout refinement and candidate selection for planning.

reference: Y. Ma, Z. Song, Y. Zhuang, J. Hao, and I. King, “A survey on vision-language-action models for embodied AI,” IEEE Trans. Neural Netw. Learn. Syst., 2026, arXiv:2405.14093.
summary: This survey organizes VLA research into model components, low-level control policies, and high-level task planners. It also reviews datasets, simulators, and benchmarks that support language-conditioned embodied action.

reference: Y. Zhong, F. Bai, S. Cai, X. Huang, Z. Chen, X. Zhang, Y. Wang, S. Guo, T. Guan, K. N. Lui et al., “A survey on vision-language-action models: An action tokenization perspective,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.01925, 2025.
summary: This survey compares VLA systems through the intermediate representations used to express actions. Its tokenization taxonomy spans language, code, affordances, trajectories, goals, latent codes, raw actions, and reasoning.

reference: K. Kawaharazuka, J. Oh, J. Yamada, I. Posner, and Y. Zhu, “Vision-language-action models for robotics: A review towards real-world applications,” IEEE Access, vol. 13, pp. 162467–162504, 2025.
summary: This review connects VLA architectures and learning methods with the practical requirements of robot deployment. It covers hardware platforms, data collection, augmentation, datasets, and evaluation alongside model design.

reference: M. U. Din, W. Akram, L. S. Saoud, J. Rosell, and I. Hussain, “Multimodal fusion with vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation: A systematic review,” Information Fusion, vol. 129, p. 104062, 2026.
summary: This systematic review organizes manipulation VLAs by multimodal fusion strategies, architectures, datasets, and evaluation resources. It also develops an agentic outlook in which planners use VLA skills with verification and diagnostic feedback.

reference: B. Hou, G. Li, J. Jia, T. An, X. Guo, S. Leng, H. Geng, Y. Ze, T. Harada, P. Torr et al., “World model for robot learning: A comprehensive survey,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.00080, 2026.
summary: This survey reviews world models according to their roles in robot-policy learning, planning, simulation, data generation, and evaluation. It relates policy coupling and controllable video prediction to datasets and experimental protocols across embodied domains.

reference: X. Li, X. He, L. Zhang, M. Wu, X. Li, and Y. Liu, “A comprehensive survey on world models for embodied AI,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.16732, 2025.
summary: This survey classifies embodied world models by functionality, temporal modeling, and spatial representation. It compares data resources and evaluation criteria while emphasizing physical consistency, temporal coherence, and computational cost.

reference: F. Wang, Z. Wang, G. Pei, M. Zhang, C. Liang, J. Hu, Z. Li, J. Wu, N. Han, Z. Zhang, J. Qi, H. Wu, S. Zhang, P. Zheng, J. Pan, D. Navarro-Alarcon, S. Liu, and P. Zhou, “World models for robotic manipulation: A survey,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.00113, 2026.
summary: This manipulation-focused survey separates predicted representations, action coupling, and the stage at which prediction is used. It distinguishes integrated prediction-action systems from explicit planners and examines evaluation of predictive fidelity and control utility.

reference: S. Wang, J. Shi, Z. Fu, X. He, F. Liu, C. Yang, Y. Zhou, Z. Fei, J. Gong, J. Fu, M. Z. Shou, X. Huang, X. Qiu, and Y.-G. Jiang, “World action models: The next frontier in embodied AI,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.12090, 2026.
summary: This survey describes world-action models as systems that combine predictive state modeling with action generation. It distinguishes cascaded and joint architectures and reviews their data requirements and evaluation dimensions.

reference: Q. Shen, S. Zhang, Y. Liao, Q. Li, Z. Tan, S. Wang, others, and X. Wang, “World action models: A survey,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.20781, 2026.
summary: This survey distinguishes world-action models by the futures they generate and how prediction is connected to actions. It compares predictive representations, backbones, deployment modes, and the trade-offs between forecast detail and control cost.

reference: R. Sapkota, Y. Cao, K. I. Roumeliotis, and M. Karkee, “Vision-language-action models: Concepts, progress, applications and challenges,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.04769, 2025.
summary: This review introduces VLA concepts and surveys architectures, training strategies, and inference methods. It examines applications across robotic domains and discusses adaptation and cross-embodiment planning challenges.

reference: R. Shao, W. Li, L. Zhang, R. Zhang, Z. Liu, R. Chen, and L. Nie, “Large VLM-based vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation: A survey,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.13073, 2025.
summary: This survey focuses on manipulation policies built on large pretrained vision-language models. It distinguishes monolithic and hierarchical architectures and reviews connections with reinforcement learning, human video, and world models.

reference: Z. Yu, B. Wang, P. Zeng, H. Zhang, J. Zhang, Z. Wang, L. Gao, J. Song, N. Sebe, and H. T. Shen, “A survey on efficient vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.24795, 2025.
summary: This survey organizes VLA efficiency research around model design, training, and robotic-data collection. It compares architectural compression and other resource-saving strategies across the learning and deployment pipeline.

reference: Deng et al., “A survey on reinforcement learning of vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation,” TechRxiv, 2025.
summary: This survey reviews reinforcement learning for adapting pretrained VLA models to robotic manipulation. It organizes architectures, online and offline learning, deployment considerations, and evaluation within a shared training-to-deployment framework.

reference: T. Feng, X. Wang, Y.-G. Jiang, and W. Zhu, “Embodied AI: From LLMs to world models,” IEEE Circuits Syst. Mag., vol. 25, no. 4, pp. 14–37, 2025, arXiv:2509.20021.
summary: This review contrasts the semantic reasoning provided by language models with the predictive capabilities of world models in embodied AI. It argues for combining these capabilities and surveys supporting technologies, hardware, and applications.

reference: K. Zhang, P. Yun, J. Cen, J. Cai, D. Zhu, H. Yuan, C. Zhao, T. Feng, M. Y. Wang, Q. Chen et al., “Generative artificial intelligence in robotic manipulation: A survey,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.03464, 2025.
summary: This survey reviews generative models used for robotic data, rewards, intermediate plans, and control outputs. Its layered taxonomy relates data generation and task reasoning to grasp and trajectory generation.

reference: J. Ding, Y. Zhang, Y. Shang, Y. Zhang, Z. Zong, J. Feng, Y. Yuan, H. Su, N. Li, N. Sukiennik et al., “Understanding world or predicting future? A comprehensive survey of world models,” ACM Comput. Surv., vol. 58, no. 3, pp. 1–38, 2025.
summary: This survey distinguishes world models that construct internal representations from those that simulate future states. It reviews these roles across robotics, autonomous driving, and other domains and identifies open modeling challenges.

reference: X. Li et al., “A step toward world models: A survey on robotic manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.02097, 2025.
summary: This survey examines manipulation methods that exhibit world-model capabilities, including approaches not explicitly labeled as world models. It uses their roles in perception, prediction, and control to identify the components needed for broader predictive robotics.

reference: Jiang et al., “A survey on vision-language-action models for autonomous driving,” in Proc. IEEE/CVF Int. Conf. Comput. Vis. Workshops (ICCVW), WDFM-AD, 2025.
summary: This survey reviews vision-language-action architectures for autonomous driving, including their progression toward reasoning-centered control. It compares vehicle-domain datasets and evaluation concerns such as safety, instruction following, and explanation quality.

reference: D. Zhang, J. Sun, C. Hu, X. Wu, Z. Yuan, R. Zhou, F. Shen, and Q. Zhou, “Pure vision language action (VLA) models: A comprehensive survey,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.19012, 2025.
summary: This survey classifies VLA methods into autoregressive, diffusion, reinforcement-learning, hybrid, and specialized approaches. It connects these design choices to application scenarios, datasets, benchmarks, and simulators.

reference: M. J. Page, J. E. McKenzie, P. M. Bossuyt, I. Boutron, T. C. Hoffmann, C. D. Mulrow, L. Shamseer, J. M. Tetzlaff, E. A. Akl, S. E. Brennan et al., “The PRISMA 2020 statement: An updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews,” BMJ, vol. 372, p. n71, 2021.
summary: The PRISMA 2020 statement provides reporting guidance for systematic reviews through checklists and flow-diagram templates. It supports transparent reporting of searches, selection, synthesis, and limitations rather than certifying that a review was conducted correctly.

reference: A. Brohan, N. Brown, J. Carbajal, Y. Chebotar, J. Dabis, C. Finn, K. Gopalakrishnan, K. Hausman, A. Herzog, J. Hsu et al., “RT-1: Robotics transformer for real-world control at scale,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2212.06817, 2022, published RSS 2023.
summary: RT-1 maps camera observations and language instructions to discretized robot commands using a transformer policy. It is an early language-conditioned control precursor to later VLA foundation models.

reference: Y. Jiang, A. Gupta, Z. Zhang, G. Wang, Y. Dou, Y. Chen, L. Fei-Fei, A. Anandkumar, Y. Zhu, and L. Fan, “VIMA: General robot manipulation with multimodal prompts,” in International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2023, arXiv:2210.03094.
summary: VIMA specifies manipulation tasks using prompts that interleave text and images. A transformer policy converts these multimodal task descriptions and observations into robot actions.

reference: X. Li, M. Liu, H. Zhang, C. Yu, J. Xu, H. Wu, C. Cheang, Y. Jing, W. Zhang, H. Liu et al., “Vision-language foundation models as effective robot imitators,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Representations (ICLR), 2024, arXiv:2311.01378.
summary: RoboFlamingo adapts a pretrained OpenFlamingo vision-language model for robot imitation learning. An action-prediction interface connects multimodal understanding to language-conditioned manipulation.

reference: D. Niu, Y. Sharma, G. Biamby, J. Quenum, Y. Bai, B. Shi, T. Darrell, and R. Herzig, “LLARVA: Vision-action instruction tuning enhances robot learning,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2024, arXiv:2406.11815.
summary: LLARVA uses vision-action instruction tuning with intermediate two-dimensional visual traces. These traces help align multimodal representations with the robot behaviors learned during adaptation.

reference: S. Ye, J. Jang, B. Jeon, S. Joo, J. Yang, B. Peng, A. Mandlekar, R. Tan et al., “Latent action pretraining from videos,” in International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2025, arXiv:2410.11758.
summary: LAPA learns latent action representations from video without ground-truth action labels during pretraining. Robot data subsequently maps the pretrained policy into executable robot actions.

reference: K. Pertsch, K. Stachowicz, B. Ichter, D. Driess, S. Nair, Q. Vuong, O. Mees, C. Finn, and S. Levine, “FAST: Efficient action tokenization for vision-language-action models,” in Proc. Robot.: Sci. Syst. (RSS), 2025, arXiv:2501.09747.
summary: FAST compresses continuous action chunks into frequency-domain tokens for autoregressive prediction. The π0-FAST policy demonstrates how this representation can support action generation for dexterous control.

reference: Liang et al., “Discrete diffusion VLA: Bringing discrete diffusion to action decoding in vision-language-action policies,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.20072, 2025.
summary: Discrete Diffusion VLA generates discretized action chunks through iterative diffusion-style refinement within a shared transformer. It explores parallel action decoding as an alternative to sequential autoregressive generation.

reference: Octo Model Team, D. Ghosh, H. Walke, K. Pertsch, K. Black, O. Mees, S. Dasari, J. Hejna, T. Kreiman, C. Xu et al., “Octo: An open-source generalist robot policy,” in Proc. Robot.: Sci. Syst. (RSS), 2024, arXiv:2405.12213.
summary: Octo is an open generalist robot policy with a diffusion action head and language- or image-goal conditioning. Its adaptation interface accommodates new observation inputs and robot action spaces.

reference: S. Liu, L. Wu, B. Li, H. Tan, H. Chen, Z. Wang, K. Xu, H. Su, and J. Zhu, “RDT-1B: A diffusion foundation model for bimanual manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.07864, 2024, published ICLR 2025.
summary: RDT-1B uses a diffusion transformer to generate bimanual robot actions conditioned on multimodal inputs. A unified action representation supports learning from robots with different configurations.

reference: Q. Li et al., “CogACT: A foundational vision-language-action model for synergizing cognition and action in robotic manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.19650, 2024.
summary: CogACT couples a vision-language backbone to a specialized diffusion action transformer. This separation connects semantic interpretation with continuous manipulation commands.

reference: J. Wen, Y. Zhu, J. Li, Z. Tang, C. Shen, and F. Feng, “DexVLA: Vision-language model with plug-in diffusion expert for general robot control,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.05855, 2025.
summary: DexVLA connects a vision-language backbone to a pretrained diffusion action expert. Its staged training adapts the action-generation component across tasks and robot embodiments.

reference: T. Z. Zhao, V. Kumar, S. Levine, and C. Finn, “Learning fine-grained bimanual manipulation with low-cost hardware,” in Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS), 2023, arXiv:2304.13705.
summary: This paper introduces the ALOHA teleoperation platform and Action Chunking with Transformers for bimanual imitation learning. Predicting sequences of actions provides a control precedent for later chunk-based VLA policies.

reference: Z. Fu, T. Z. Zhao, and C. Finn, “Mobile ALOHA: Learning bimanual mobile manipulation with low-cost whole-body teleoperation,” in Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2024, arXiv:2401.02117.
summary: Mobile ALOHA combines whole-body teleoperation with imitation learning for mobile bimanual manipulation. It extends demonstration-based control to coordinated base and arm motions.

reference: C. Chi, Z. Xu, S. Feng, E. Cousineau, Y. Du, B. Burchfiel, R. Tedrake, and S. Song, “Diffusion policy: Visuomotor policy learning via action diffusion,” in Proc. Robot.: Sci. Syst. (RSS), 2023, arXiv:2303.04137.
summary: Diffusion Policy models visuomotor action sequences through conditional denoising diffusion. Receding-horizon execution makes it a control foundation for later diffusion-based robot policies.

reference: Physical Intelligence, K. Black, N. Brown, J. Darpinian, K. Dhabalia, D. Driess, A. Esmail, M. Equi, C. Finn, N. Fusai et al., “π0.5: A vision-language-action model with open-world generalization,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.16054, 2025.
summary: The π0.5 model extends π0 through heterogeneous co-training and hierarchical task conditioning. It studies language-conditioned manipulation in settings beyond familiar training environments.

reference: Figure AI, “Helix: A vision-language-action model for generalist humanoid control,” Figure AI technical blog, , 2025.
summary: Helix combines a slower vision-language component with a faster continuous-action controller for humanoid upper-body manipulation. The cited vendor release describes this dual-system architecture and its demonstrated behaviors.

reference: M. Ahn, A. Brohan, N. Brown, Y. Chebotar, O. Cortes, B. David, C. Finn, C. Fu, K. Gopalakrishnan, K. Hausman et al., “Do as I can, not as I say: Grounding language in robotic affordances,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2022, arXiv:2204.01691.
summary: SayCan combines language-model task suggestions with learned skill-value estimates. It uses these estimates to select behaviors that are both instruction-relevant and physically feasible.

reference: D. Driess, F. Xia, M. S. M. Sajjadi, C. Lynch, A. Chowdhery, B. Ichter, A. Wahid, J. Tompson, Q. Vuong, T. Yu et al., “PaLM-E: An embodied multimodal language model,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Mach. Learn. (ICML), 2023, arXiv:2303.03378.
summary: PaLM-E incorporates visual observations and continuous sensor information into an embodied language model. It supports multimodal reasoning and high-level robot planning.

reference: S. Belkhale, T. Ding, T. Xiao, P. Sermanet, Q. Vuong, J. Tompson, Y. Chebotar, D. Dwibedi, and D. Sadigh, “RT-H: Action hierarchies using language,” in Proc. Robot.: Sci. Syst. (RSS), 2024, arXiv:2403.01823.
summary: RT-H inserts a language-based action hierarchy between task instructions and low-level robot commands. Intermediate motion descriptions organize execution and provide a structured interface for control.

reference: J. Liang, W. Huang, F. Xia, P. Xu, K. Hausman, B. Ichter, P. Florence, and A. Zeng, “Code as policies: Language model programs for embodied control,” in IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), 2023, arXiv:2209.07753.
summary: Code as Policies generates robot-control programs from natural-language instructions. The generated programs connect perception outputs, control APIs, and feedback to executable behaviors.

reference: W. Huang, C. Wang, R. Zhang, Y. Li, J. Wu, and L. Fei-Fei, “VoxPoser: Composable 3D value maps for robotic manipulation with language models,” in Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2023, arXiv:2307.05973.
summary: VoxPoser converts language and visual information into composable three-dimensional value maps. These maps guide motion planning for manipulation instead of directly predicting motor commands from a single policy head.

reference: L. X. Shi et al., “Hi robot: Open-ended instruction following with hierarchical vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.19417, 2025.
summary: Hi Robot uses hierarchical vision-language-action policies to interpret complex instructions and user feedback. A lower-level controller executes the manipulation steps selected by the higher-level reasoning component.

reference: M. Zawalski, W. Chen, K. Pertsch, O. Mees, C. Finn, and S. Levine, “Robotic control via embodied chain-of-thought reasoning,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2024, arXiv:2407.08693.
summary: Embodied Chain-of-Thought trains a VLA to generate intermediate plans and visually grounded reasoning before robot actions. The method studies whether explicit reasoning supervision improves control and instruction execution.

reference: Lin et al., “OneTwoVLA: A unified vision-language-action model with adaptive reasoning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.11917, 2025.
summary: OneTwoVLA unifies explicit reasoning and robot-action generation within one model. It switches between reasoning and execution as task progress requires.

reference: Song et al., “RationalVLA: A rational vision-language-action model with dual system,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.10826, 2025.
summary: RationalVLA couples higher-level instruction reasoning with manipulation control in a dual-system design. It includes assessment and rejection of commands judged infeasible or defective.

reference: W. Huang, C. Wang, Y. Li, R. Zhang, and L. Fei-Fei, “ReKep: Spatio-temporal reasoning of relational keypoint constraints for robotic manipulation,” in Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2024, arXiv:2409.01652.
summary: ReKep uses visual-language reasoning to formulate relational constraints between task-relevant keypoints. It then optimizes robot motions to satisfy those constraints over time.

reference: F. Liu, K. Fang, P. Abbeel, and S. Levine, “MOKA: Open-world robotic manipulation through mark-based visual prompting,” in Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS), 2024, arXiv:2403.03174.
summary: MOKA uses marked images and point-based affordances to interpret manipulation instructions. These geometric interfaces translate vision-language reasoning into executable control commands.

reference: Q. Zhao et al., “CoT-VLA: Visual chain-of-thought reasoning for vision-language-action models,” in Proc. IEEE/CVF Conf. Comput. Vis. Pattern Recognit. (CVPR), 2025, arXiv:2503.22020.
summary: CoT-VLA predicts future images as intermediate visual goals before generating action sequences. This visual chain of thought links prediction to policy execution without itself establishing candidate-action search.

reference: M. U. Din, J. Rosell, W. Akram, I. Zaplana, M. A. Roa, L. Seneviratne, and I. Hussain, “Ontology-driven prompt tuning for LLM-based task and motion planning,” Robot. Auton. Syst., 2025.
summary: This framework enriches language-model prompts with ontology-based task knowledge and descriptions of the environment. It uses this knowledge to improve semantic consistency and temporal ordering in task-and-motion plans.

reference: M. Shridhar, L. Manuelli, and D. Fox, “Perceiver-Actor: A multi-task transformer for robotic manipulation,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2022, arXiv:2209.05451.
summary: PerAct encodes language goals and voxelized RGB-D observations with a Perceiver architecture. It learns discretized six-degree-of-freedom manipulation actions through behavior cloning.

reference: A. Goyal, J. Xu, Y. Guo, V. Blukis, Y.-W. Chao, and D. Fox, “RVT: Robotic view transformer for 3D object manipulation,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2023, arXiv:2306.14896.
summary: RVT combines rendered views of a three-dimensional scene with language-goal embeddings in a transformer. The resulting representation supports spatially grounded manipulation from limited demonstrations.

reference: A. Goyal, V. Blukis, J. Xu, Y. Guo, Y.-W. Chao, and D. Fox, “RVT-2: Learning precise manipulation from few demonstrations,” in Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS), 2024, arXiv:2406.08545.
summary: RVT-2 improves the architecture and execution of language-conditioned multi-view manipulation policies. It emphasizes precise control and efficient learning from few demonstrations.

reference: T. Gervet, Z. Xian, N. Gkanatsios, and K. Fragkiadaki, “Act3D: 3D feature field transformers for multi-task robotic manipulation,” in Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2023, arXiv:2306.17817.
summary: Act3D uses a hierarchical three-dimensional feature field with task-instruction conditioning to predict manipulation actions. Coarse-to-fine spatial sampling concentrates computation where precise action prediction is needed.

reference: H. Zhen, X. Qiu, P. Chen, J. Yang, X. Yan, Y. Du, Y. Hong, and C. Gan, “3D-VLA: A 3D vision-language-action generative world model,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Mach. Learn. (ICML), 2024, arXiv:2403.09631.
summary: 3D-VLA combines three-dimensional vision-language representations with generation of future observations and robot actions. It connects spatial grounding with predictive policy learning for manipulation.

reference: D. Qu, H. Song, Q. Chen, Y. Yao, X. Ye, Y. Ding, Z. Wang, J. Gu, B. Zhao, D. Wang et al., “SpatialVLA: Exploring spatial representations for visual-language-action models,” in Proc. Robot.: Sci. Syst. (RSS), 2025, arXiv:2501.15830.
summary: SpatialVLA uses geometric visual representations and spatially structured action tokens. These representations connect scene geometry with language-conditioned manipulation commands.

reference: Li et al., “PointVLA: Injecting the 3D world into vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.07511, 2025.
summary: PointVLA injects point-cloud information into pretrained VLA action modules through lightweight adaptation. It gives an existing policy access to three-dimensional geometry for manipulation.

reference: Jia et al., “Lift3D foundation policy: Lifting 2D large-scale pretrained models for robust 3D robotic manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.18623, 2024.
summary: Lift3D adapts pretrained two-dimensional visual features into implicit and explicit three-dimensional manipulation representations. Its reported policy uses point clouds and robot state without language conditioning.

reference: Yang et al., “FP3: A 3D foundation policy for robotic manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.08950, 2025.
summary: FP3 pretrains a diffusion-transformer manipulation policy using point clouds, proprioception, and CLIP-encoded instructions. It adapts this language-conditioned three-dimensional policy to downstream tasks.

reference: Li et al., “BridgeVLA: Input-output alignment for efficient 3D manipulation learning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.07961, 2025.
summary: BridgeVLA projects three-dimensional observations into multiple image views and predicts spatial action heatmaps. This design aligns visual inputs with the spatial representation of control outputs.

reference: S. Deng, M. Yan, S. Wei, H. Ma, Y. Yang, J. Chen, Z. Zhang, T. Yang, X. Zhang, W. Zhang, H. Cui, Z. Zhang, and H. Wang, “GraspVLA: A grasping foundation model pre-trained on billion-scale synthetic action data,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.03233, 2025.
summary: GraspVLA combines autoregressive perception with flow-matching action generation for grasping. Its training integrates synthetic robot data with semantic pretraining to support generalizable grasp behavior.

reference: Sun et al., “GeoVLA: Empowering 3D representations in vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.09071, 2025.
summary: GeoVLA fuses image-language representations with point-cloud geometry in an action expert. This spatial interface supplies three-dimensional context for language-conditioned manipulation.

reference: Bhat et al., “3D CAVLA: Leveraging depth and 3D context to generalize vision-language-action models for unseen tasks,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.05800, 2025.
summary: 3D-CAVLA combines depth information, task-relevant visual regions, and intermediate reasoning for VLA adaptation. These cues support manipulation in tasks beyond those seen during training.

reference: Y. Guo et al., “Improving vision-language-action model with online reinforcement learning,” in Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. Robot. Autom. (ICRA), 2025, arXiv:2501.16664.
summary: iRe-VLA alternates reinforcement-learning improvement with supervised learning. This alternating procedure aims to stabilize interactive adaptation of pretrained VLA policies.

reference: Z. Zhang et al., “GRAPE: Generalizing robot policy via preference alignment,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.19309, 2024.
summary: GRAPE aligns robot policies using trajectory preferences derived from successful and unsuccessful behavior. Task-specific spatial and temporal constraints guide the preference-based training signal.

reference: Xu et al., “RLDG: Robotic generalist policy distillation via reinforcement learning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2412.09858, 2024.
summary: RLDG distills trajectories produced by task-specific reinforcement-learning policies into a generalist robot policy. It uses specialist behavior as an additional source of training data for generalist control.

reference: Chen et al., “ConRFT: A reinforced fine-tuning method for VLA models via consistency policy,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.05450, 2025.
summary: ConRFT fine-tunes VLA policies through offline and online reinforcement learning with a consistency-based objective. Human intervention during online learning supports adaptation to physical manipulation tasks.

reference: Lu et al., “VLA-RL: Towards masterful and general robotic manipulation with scalable reinforcement learning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.18719, 2025.
summary: VLA-RL applies online reinforcement learning to autoregressive VLA policies. Its framework combines scalable training infrastructure with a learned progress-reward model.

reference: J. Hu, R. Hendrix, A. Farhadi, A. Kembhavi, R. Martín-Martín, P. Stone, K.-H. Zeng, and K. Ehsani, “FLaRe: Achieving masterful and adaptive robot policies with large-scale reinforcement learning fine-tuning,” in Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. Robot. Autom. (ICRA), 2025, arXiv:2409.16578.
summary: FLaRe uses large-scale reinforcement-learning fine-tuning to improve pretrained robot policies. It is distinct from FLARE, the separate method for aligning policy features with future latent representations.

reference: J. Wen, Y. Zhu, J. Li, M. Zhu, K. Wu, Z. Xu, N. Liu, R. Cheng, C. Shen, Y. Peng et al., “TinyVLA: Towards fast, data-efficient vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation,” IEEE Robot. Autom. Lett., 2025, arXiv:2409.12514.
summary: TinyVLA combines a compact multimodal backbone with a diffusion action decoder. It targets manipulation learning with lower computation and fewer demonstrations.

reference: M. Shukor, D. Aubakirova, F. Capuano, P. Kooijmans, S. Palma, A. Zouitine, M. Aractingi, C. Pascal, M. Russi, A. Marafioti et al., “SmolVLA: A vision-language-action model for affordable and efficient robotics,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.01844, 2025.
summary: SmolVLA uses a compact vision-language backbone and a flow-matching action expert. Its asynchronous inference design supports robot deployment with modest computational resources.

reference: Budzianowski et al., “EdgeVLA: Efficient vision-language-action models for edge deployment,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.14049, 2025.
summary: EdgeVLA combines a smaller language backbone with non-autoregressive action prediction. It targets reduced inference and memory costs on resource-constrained robot hardware.

reference: J. Liu, M. Liu, Z. Wang, L. Lee, K. Zhou, P. An, S. Yang, R. Zhang, Y. Guo, and S. Zhang, “RoboMamba: Multimodal state space model for efficient robot reasoning and manipulation,” in Adv. Neural Inf. Process. Syst. (NeurIPS), 2024, arXiv:2406.04339.
summary: RoboMamba uses a Mamba state-space backbone for multimodal reasoning and robot-action prediction. It explores efficient language-conditioned manipulation through this alternative sequence-model architecture.

reference: H. Wang, C. Xiong, R. Wang, and X. Chen, “BitVLA: 1-bit vision-language-action models for robotics manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.07530, 2025.
summary: BitVLA combines low-bit model weights with visual-encoder compression to reduce the memory and inference demands of a VLA policy. It addresses resource-efficient manipulation deployment rather than explicit prediction of action consequences.

reference: Xu et al., “VLA-Cache: Towards efficient vision-language-action model via adaptive token caching,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.02175, 2025.
summary: VLA-Cache reuses visual tokens that change little between observations while recomputing task-relevant information. This reduces repeated inference work in an existing VLA control pipeline.

reference: Yang et al., “EfficientVLA: Training-free acceleration and compression for vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.10100, 2025.
summary: EfficientVLA accelerates existing policies through language-layer pruning, visual-token selection, and reuse of diffusion-head features. Its contribution is a training-free reduction of policy inference cost.

reference: Song et al., “Accelerating vision-language-action model integrated with action chunking via parallel decoding,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.02310, 2025.
summary: PD-VLA applies parallel fixed-point iterations to decode action chunks from an autoregressive VLA. It targets action-generation latency while retaining the policy formulation of robot control.

reference: –––, “CEED-VLA: Consistency vision-language-action model with early-exit decoding,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.13725, 2025.
summary: CEED-VLA uses consistency distillation and early-exit decoding to accelerate action-token generation. It studies efficient execution of VLA policies under constrained inference budgets.

reference: Y. Yue, Y. Wang, B. Kang, Y. Han, S. Wang, S. Song, J. Feng, and G. Huang, “DeeR-VLA: Dynamic inference of multimodal large language models for efficient robot execution,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2024, arXiv:2411.02359.
summary: DeeR-VLA equips a multimodal policy backbone with multiple exits so that inference depth can vary with the current input. It links robot execution efficiency to adaptive computation rather than a fixed processing depth.

reference: Google DeepMind, “Gemini Robotics On-Device: Bringing AI to local robotic devices,” Google DeepMind announcement, 2025.
summary: Gemini Robotics On-Device is a vendor-reported VLA designed to run locally on robot hardware. The release describes adaptation to manipulation tasks through fine-tuning and provides context for on-device deployment.

reference: J. Chen, H. Liang, L. Du, W. Wang, M. Hu, Y. Mu, W. Wang, J. Dai, P. Luo, W. Shao, and L. Shao, “OWMM-Agent: Open world mobile manipulation with multi-modal agentic data synthesis,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2025, arXiv:2506.04217.
summary: OWMM-Agent uses multimodal scene and robot-state context to coordinate mobile manipulation through function calls. Its associated instruction tuning supports an agentic integration of perception, navigation, and manipulation components.

reference: P. Liu, Y. Orru, J. Vakil, C. Paxton, N. M. M. Shafiullah, and L. Pinto, “OK-Robot: What really matters in integrating open-knowledge models for robotics,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2401.12202, 2024.
summary: OK-Robot integrates open perception, navigation, and grasping components for language-directed mobile manipulation. It studies how these components work together in unfamiliar environments.

reference: Fan et al., “Long-VLA: Unleashing long-horizon capability of vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.19958, 2025.
summary: Long-VLA uses phase-aware masking of sensory inputs to support coordination across successive subtasks. It addresses error accumulation and execution over extended manipulation horizons.

reference: Yang et al., “LoHoVLA: A unified vision-language-action model for long-horizon embodied tasks,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.00411, 2025.
summary: LoHoVLA jointly generates subtask language and robot-action tokens. Hierarchical feedback connects these outputs during multi-step embodied task execution.

reference: NVIDIA GEAR Lab, “GR00T N1.5: An improved open foundation model for generalist humanoid robots,” NVIDIA Research, , 2025.
summary: GR00T N1.5 extends the GR00T humanoid policy family with changes to its architecture and training data. The official release describes future-latent representation alignment as a component of policy learning.

reference: NVIDIA, “GR00T-N1.7-3B model card,” Hugging Face, 2026, accessed: Sep. 30, 2026.
summary: GR00T N1.7 is a cross-embodiment robot policy that conditions action chunks on visual observations, language, and proprioception. Its released model uses a flow-matching action transformer and supports post-training for particular robots and tasks.

reference: Physical Intelligence, B. Ai, A. Amin, R. Aniceto, A. Balakrishna, G. Balke, K. Black, G. Bokinsky, S. Cao, T. Charbonnier et al., “π0.7: A steerable generalist robotic foundation model with emergent capabilities,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.15483, 2026.
summary: π0.7 conditions a generalist robot policy on language and additional context such as subgoal images and task-performance metadata. This conditioning supports steering the execution strategy while training on demonstrations, autonomous experience, and non-robot data.

reference: W. Wu, F. Wang, F. Lu, H. Sun, S. Liu, Y. Wang, Y. Yan, Y. Wang, S. Ma, X. Wang, Y. Liu, S. Yang, T. Zhou, K. Zhang, L. Zhou, C. Su, N. Xue, B. Tan, H. Zhang, Y. Zhang, F. Liao, X. Zhu, Y. Shen, and K. Zheng, “From foundation to application: Improving VLA models in practice,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.06403, 2026.
summary: LingBot-VLA 2.0 extends a generalist VLA with whole-body action spaces and training across multiple robot embodiments and human videos. Auxiliary future prediction uses video-representation and depth-estimation supervision to connect action learning with temporal and geometric information.

reference: C.-L. Cheang, G. Chen, Y. Jing, T. Kong, H. Li, Y. Li, Y. Liu, H. Wu, J. Xu, Y. Yang et al., “GR-2: A generative video-language-action model with web-scale knowledge for robot manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.06158, 2024.
summary: GR-2 combines large-scale video pretraining with joint video and action learning for robotic manipulation. Its predictive-policy formulation connects visual knowledge from web video to robot trajectories.

reference: Figure AI, “Introducing Helix 02: Full-body autonomy,” Figure technical blog, Jan. 2026, jan. 27, 2026. Accessed: Sep. 30, 2026.
summary: Helix 02 combines language and scene reasoning, a full-body visuomotor policy, and a learned low-level whole-body controller. The vendor describes coordinated locomotion and manipulation using visual, tactile, and proprioceptive inputs.

reference: S. Ross, G. J. Gordon, and J. A. Bagnell, “A reduction of imitation learning and structured prediction to no-regret online learning,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Artif. Intell. Statist. (AISTATS), 2011.
summary: DAgger addresses imitation-learning distribution shift by iteratively collecting expert labels on states encountered by the learner. The paper connects this data-aggregation procedure to no-regret online learning and sequential prediction.

reference: A. Khazatsky, K. Pertsch, S. Nair, A. Balakrishna, S. Dasari, S. Karamcheti, S. Nasiriany, M. K. Srirama, L. Y. Chen, K. Ellis et al., “DROID: A large-scale in-the-wild robot manipulation dataset,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2403.12945, 2024, published RSS 2024.
summary: DROID provides diverse real-world robot manipulation demonstrations collected across environments. It supports research on policy learning and generalization from robot observations and actions.

reference: NVIDIA, “Cosmos world foundation model platform for physical AI,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2501.03575, 2025.
summary: Cosmos provides video tokenization and generative world foundation models for physical-AI development. Action conditioning and robot-control use depend on the particular model and its adaptation.

reference: S. Motamed, L. Culp, K. Swersky, P. Jaini, and R. Geirhos, “Do generative video models understand physical laws?” in Proc. IEEE/CVF Int. Conf. Comput. Vis. (ICCV), 2025, arXiv:2501.09038.
summary: Physics-IQ evaluates physical prediction using paired real videos rather than visual plausibility alone. It supplies evidence about physical consistency in generative video models without directly measuring robot-control success.

reference: Li et al., “WorldModelBench: Judging video generation models as world models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.20694, 2025.
summary: WorldModelBench evaluates instruction-conditioned video generation against physical principles. It assesses properties of generated worlds rather than serving as a direct manipulation-policy success benchmark.

reference: Z. Huang et al., “VBench-2.0: Advancing video generation benchmark suite for intrinsic faithfulness,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2503.21755, 2025.
summary: VBench-2.0 evaluates generated video for human fidelity, controllability, creativity, physics, and commonsense. Its metrics target intrinsic faithfulness beyond surface visual plausibility.

reference: X. Li, K. Hsu, J. Gu, K. Pertsch, O. Mees, H. R. Walke, C. Fu, I. Lunawat, I. Sieh, S. Kirmani et al., “Evaluating real-world robot manipulation policies in simulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.05941, 2024.
summary: SimplerEnv constructs simulated evaluations intended to correspond to physical robot manipulation settings. It studies how closely policy performance in these simulations tracks real-world evaluation.

reference: R. Cui, Z. Zhang, J. Pang, H. Chi, J. Guo, S. Zhang, S. Xie, X. Jin, Y. Mu, J. Yang, G. Yao, X. Zhan, Y.-Q. Zhang, and H. Zhao, “LIBERO-Safety: A comprehensive benchmark for physical and semantic safety in vision-language-action models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.23686, 2026.
summary: LIBERO-Safety procedurally generates safety-critical manipulation scenarios and accompanying collision-free demonstrations. It evaluates physical and semantic safety properties of embodied policies under task constraints.

reference: A. Z. Ren, A. Dixit, A. Bodrova, S. Singh, S. Tu, N. Brown, P. Xu, L. Takayama, F. Xia, J. Varley et al., “Robots that ask for help: Uncertainty alignment for large language model planners,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2023, arXiv:2307.01928.
summary: KnowNo uses conformal prediction to calibrate uncertainty in language-model planning. The framework uses this uncertainty to determine when a robot should request human assistance.

reference: A. D. Ames, S. Coogan, M. Egerstedt, G. Notomista, K. Sreenath, and P. Tabuada, “Control barrier functions: Theory and applications,” in Proc. Eur. Control Conf. (ECC), 2019.
summary: This overview explains how control barrier functions can verify and enforce safety properties of dynamical systems. It connects the theory to optimization-based safety-critical controllers and robotic applications.

reference: S. Bansal, M. Chen, S. Herbert, and C. J. Tomlin, “Hamilton–Jacobi reachability: A brief overview and recent advances,” in Proc. IEEE Conf. Decis. Control (CDC), 2017.
summary: This tutorial reviews Hamilton-Jacobi reachability for analyzing safety and performance of nonlinear dynamical systems with bounded disturbances. It also discusses numerical tools and approaches to the computational difficulty of high-dimensional systems.

reference: D. Ha and J. Schmidhuber, “World models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:1803.10122, 2018.
summary: World Models combines a variational image encoder, recurrent latent dynamics, and a compact controller. It demonstrates learning behavior within a learned environment in simulated control tasks.

reference: D. Hafner, T. Lillicrap, I. Fischer, R. Villegas, D. Ha, H. Lee, and J. Davidson, “Learning latent dynamics for planning from pixels,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Mach. Learn. (ICML), 2019, arXiv:1811.04551.
summary: PlaNet learns action-conditioned recurrent latent dynamics from images. It uses model-predictive control to select action sequences by evaluating imagined futures.

reference: D. Hafner, J. Pasukonis, J. Ba, and T. Lillicrap, “Mastering diverse control tasks through world models,” Nature, vol. 640, pp. 647–653, 2025.
summary: DreamerV3 learns policies and value functions through trajectories imagined in a latent dynamics model. Its training design aims to support varied control domains with a common configuration.

reference: J. Schrittwieser, I. Antonoglou, T. Hubert, K. Simonyan, L. Sifre, S. Schmitt, A. Guez, E. Lockhart, D. Hassabis, T. Graepel et al., “Mastering Atari, Go, chess and shogi by planning with a learned model,” Nature, vol. 588, pp. 604–609, 2020.
summary: MuZero learns latent transitions that predict rewards, values, and action priors for tree search. Its cited demonstrations concern games, with planning-relevant prediction that does not require observation reconstruction.

reference: N. Hansen, H. Su, and X. Wang, “TD-MPC2: Scalable, robust world models for continuous control,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Representations (ICLR), 2024, arXiv:2310.16828.
summary: TD-MPC2 learns task-conditioned latent dynamics and value functions for continuous control. These predictions support model-predictive control across multiple tasks.

reference: Y. Du, S. Yang, B. Dai, H. Dai, O. Nachum, J. B. Tenenbaum, D. Schuurmans, and P. Abbeel, “Learning universal policies via text-guided video generation,” in Adv. Neural Inf. Process. Syst. (NeurIPS), 2023.
summary: UniPi generates a language-conditioned video plan and recovers executable actions through inverse dynamics. The generated plan is a visual action proposal rather than a forward prediction conditioned on supplied candidate robot actions.

reference: S. Yang, Y. Du, K. Ghasemipour, J. Tompson, L. Kaelbling, D. Schuurmans, and P. Abbeel, “Learning interactive real-world simulators,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Representations (ICLR), 2024.
summary: UniSim learns an interactive video simulator that responds to high-level instructions or low-level controls. It supports policy learning and evaluation through generated environment interactions.

reference: P.-C. Ko, J. Mao, Y. Du, S.-H. Sun, and J. B. Tenenbaum, “Learning to act from actionless videos through dense correspondences,” in International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024, arXiv:2310.08576.
summary: AVDC generates task-directed videos and uses dense correspondences between frames to infer control actions. This connects action-free video demonstrations to robot execution.

reference: K. Black, M. Nakamoto, P. Atreya, H. Walke, C. Finn, A. Kumar, and S. Levine, “Zero-shot robotic manipulation with pretrained image-editing diffusion models,” in International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024, arXiv:2310.10639.
summary: SuSIE adapts an image-editing diffusion model to propose visual subgoals from an observation and language instruction. A goal-conditioned controller executes the proposed subgoals.

reference: Y. Du, S. Yang, P. Florence, F. Xia, A. Wahid, B. Ichter, P. Sermanet, T. Yu, P. Abbeel, J. B. Tenenbaum, L. Kaelbling, A. Zeng, and J. Tompson, “Video language planning,” in International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2024, arXiv:2310.10625.
summary: Video Language Planning searches over language proposals and generated video continuations using vision-language policies and value functions. A goal-conditioned policy executes the resulting visual plan.

reference: J. Wu, S. Yin, N. Feng, X. He, D. Li, J. Hao, and M. Long, “iVideoGPT: Interactive VideoGPTs are scalable world models,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2024, arXiv:2405.15223.
summary: iVideoGPT autoregressively models tokenized observations, actions, and rewards. Its learned dynamics support interactive video prediction, visual planning, and model-based reinforcement learning.

reference: H. Wu, Y. Jing, C. Cheang, G. Chen, J. Xu, X. Li, M. Liu, H. Li, and T. Kong, “Unleashing large-scale video generative pre-training for visual robot manipulation,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Learn. Representations (ICLR), 2024, arXiv:2312.13139.
summary: GR-1 predicts future images and robot actions from language, visual history, and robot state after video pretraining. This shared predictive-policy training is distinct from searching over supplied candidate actions during deployment.

reference: J. Bruce, M. Dennis, A. Edwards, J. Parker-Holder, Y. Shi, E. Hughes, M. Lai, A. Mavalankar, R. Steigerwald, C. Apps et al., “Genie: Generative interactive environments,” in Proc. Int. Conf. Mach. Learn. (ICML), 2024, arXiv:2402.15391.
summary: Genie learns latent actions and interactive video dynamics from unlabelled video. Its generated environments respond to controls, providing a precursor for learned interactive simulation.

reference: Google DeepMind, “Genie 3: A new frontier for world models,” Google DeepMind announcement, 2025.
summary: Genie 3 generates interactive visual environments that respond to user controls. The cited research announcement concerns environment generation rather than validated physical robot dynamics.

reference: Liao et al., “Genie envisioner: A unified world foundation platform for robotic manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.05635, 2025.
summary: Genie Envisioner connects instruction-conditioned video modeling, action generation, and learned simulation within one platform. Its GE-Base, GE-Act, and GE-Sim components serve different predictive and control roles.

reference: M. Assran, Q. Duval, I. Misra, P. Bojanowski, P. Vincent, M. Rabbat, Y. LeCun, and N. Ballas, “Self-supervised learning from images with a joint-embedding predictive architecture,” in Proc. IEEE/CVF Conf. Comput. Vis. Pattern Recognit. (CVPR), 2023.
summary: I-JEPA learns image representations by predicting target-region embeddings from visible context. It is a representation-learning precursor rather than a temporal, action-conditioned robot dynamics model.

reference: A. Bardes, Q. Garrido, J. Ponce, X. Chen, M. Rabbat, Y. LeCun, M. Assran, and N. Ballas, “Revisiting feature prediction for learning visual representations from video,” Trans. Mach. Learn. Res. (TMLR), 2024.
summary: V-JEPA learns video representations by predicting masked spatiotemporal features. Its action-free pretraining provides predictive representations without directly defining a robot-action-conditioned forward model.

reference: G. Zhou, H. Pan, Y. LeCun, and L. Pinto, “DINO-WM: World models on pre-trained visual features enable zero-shot planning,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.04983, 2024.
summary: DINO-WM learns action-conditioned transitions over pretrained DINO image features. It plans toward visual goals in feature space without reconstructing future images.

reference: J. Chen, K. Wang, K. Chen, S. Chen, F. Gao, W. Tang, Z. Li, W. Liu, Z. Yao, B. Li, Y. Xu, and C. Yu, “LaWAM: Latent world action models for efficient dynamics-aware robot policies,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.15768, 2026.
summary: LaWAM predicts latent visual subgoals and conditions robot-action generation on them. It incorporates predictive information into a policy without requiring dense future-image generation.

reference: J. Sun, W. Zhang, Z. Qi, S. Ren, Z. Liu, H. Zhu, G. Sun, X. Jin, and Z. Chen, “VLA-JEPA: Enhancing vision-language-action model with latent world model,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.10098, 2026.
summary: VLA-JEPA pretrains a policy backbone to predict future latent states from current observations. It subsequently adapts an action head, with future frames serving as training targets rather than inputs to the prediction pathway.

reference: H. Zhen, Q. Sun, H. Zhang, J. Li, S. Zhou, Y. Du, and C. Gan, “TesserAct: Learning 4D embodied world models,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.20995, 2025.
summary: TesserAct predicts RGB, depth, and surface-normal video to represent how three-dimensional scenes evolve. Its multimodal predictions also support learning inverse dynamics for embodied tasks.

reference: G. Lu, B. Jia, P. Li, Y. Chen, Z. Wang, Y. Tang, and S. Huang, “GWM: Towards scalable gaussian world models for robotic manipulation,” in IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 2025, pp. 9263–9274.
summary: GWM models action-conditioned manipulation dynamics using Gaussian scene representations. The paper studies this representation for predictive pretraining and learned simulation.

reference: G. Lu, S. Zhang, Z. Wang, C. Liu, J. Lu, and Y. Tang, “ManiGaussian: Dynamic gaussian splatting for multi-task robotic manipulation,” in European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 2024, arXiv:2403.08321.
summary: ManiGaussian uses dynamic Gaussian representations and future-scene reconstruction as predictive supervision for manipulation. Its language-conditioned policy evaluation is conducted in RLBench simulation.

reference: T. Zhang, H.-X. Yu, R. Wu, B. Y. Feng, C. Zheng, N. Snavely, J. Wu, and W. T. Freeman, “PhysDreamer: Physics-based interaction with 3D objects via video generation,” in European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 2024, arXiv:2404.13026.
summary: PhysDreamer distills motion information from video generation into physical material estimates and interactive three-dimensional dynamics. Its object-response demonstrations provide context for physical prediction rather than direct evidence of robot task success.

reference: S. Wu et al., “Tactile-WAM: Touch-aware world action model with tactile asymmetric attention,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.26663, 2026.
summary: Tactile-WAM jointly models visual, tactile, and action information with tactile asymmetric attention. It directs contact information toward action prediction while limiting interference with video generation.

reference: J. Zhou, F. Hong, Y. Li, Y. Zhao, Y. Cen, Z. Liu, J. Huang, Z. Chen, R. Zhang, W. Zhu et al., “TouchWorld: A predictive and reactive tactile foundation model for dexterous manipulation,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.07287, 2026.
summary: TouchWorld combines predicted tactile subgoals and visuomotor action chunks with a faster tactile and proprioceptive correction policy. This joins predictive and reactive control for contact-rich dexterous manipulation.

reference: A. Mandlekar, S. Nasiriany, B. Wen, I. Akinola, Y. Narang, L. Fan, Y. Zhu, and D. Fox, “MimicGen: A data generation system for scalable robot learning using human demonstrations,” in Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2023, arXiv:2310.17596.
summary: MimicGen transforms and recombines human demonstrations to generate additional robot trajectories in conventional simulation. It is a demonstration-expansion pipeline rather than a learned environment dynamics model.

reference: Z. Jiang, Y. Xie, K. Lin, Z. Xu, W. Wan, A. Mandlekar, L. Fan, and Y. Zhu, “DexMimicGen: Automated data generation for bimanual dexterous manipulation via imitation learning,” in IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), 2025, arXiv:2410.24185.
summary: DexMimicGen extends demonstration-based data generation to bimanual dexterous manipulation in simulation. It handles coordination between manipulators when synthesizing trajectories for imitation learning.

reference: Y. Li, Y. Zhu, J. Wen, C. Shen, and Y. Xu, “WorldEval: World model as real-world robot policies evaluator,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.19017, 2025.
summary: WorldEval adapts video generation to action-following simulation using Policy2Vec. It evaluates robot policies through generated rollouts instead of requiring each evaluation to run on hardware.

reference: A. K. Sharma, Y. Sun, N. Lu, Y. Zhang, J. Liu, and S. Yang, “World-Gymnast: Training robots with reinforcement learning in a world model,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.02454, 2026.
summary: World-Gymnast trains robot policies with reinforcement learning inside a learned environment and tests transfer to hardware. Its physical-task comparisons provide evidence about the complete training-and-simulation package rather than isolating every component.

reference: R. Zheng, J. Wang, S. Reed, J. Bjorck, Y. Fang, F. Hu, J. Jang, K. Kundalia, Z. Lin, L. Magne et al., “FLARE: Robot learning with implicit world modeling,” in Proc. Conf. Robot Learn. (CoRL), 2025, arXiv:2505.15659.
summary: FLARE aligns policy features with embeddings of future observations to incorporate latent prediction into diffusion-based action learning. It also supports co-training with action-free video and is distinct from the reinforcement-learning method FLaRe.

reference: Zhang et al., “DreamVLA: A vision-language-action model dreamed with comprehensive world knowledge,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.04447, 2025.
